name: eventpp::SpinLock (eventpp GeneralThreading policy)
workload: EventQueue enqueue/process microbenchmark: N enqueue threads and N process threads (1 to 16) moving 10M events across 100 event types/listeners, protected by either std::mutex or eventpp::SpinLock as the Threading::Mutex policy.
claimed_speedup: 1 enqueue/1 process thread: SpinLock 1303ms vs std::mutex 1824ms (~1.4x faster). 2/2 threads: 3049ms vs 3151ms (slightly faster). 4/4 threads (= CPU core count): 1659ms vs 1657ms (essentially tied). 16/16 threads: 1891ms vs 708ms (SpinLock ~2.7x SLOWER). Verbatim table from doc/benchmark.md.
compiler_and_flags: MinGW GCC 11.3.0 (stated default compiler for this table; MSVC 2022 also used elsewhere in the same doc for other tables; optimization flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i5-8300H @ 2.30GHz, 16GB RAM, Windows 10 (per doc/benchmark.md, described by the author as 'pretty medium to low end')
tradeoffs: SpinLock busy-waits (burns CPU) instead of blocking via the kernel; degrades badly under thread oversubscription; only a real win when thread count is at or below the physical core count; not a safe general drop-in replacement for std::mutex.
caveats: First-party benchmark; the doc states CPU model and compilers used but not optimization flags, so per the evidence-tier rules this is capped at C even though methodology is otherwise fairly complete. Results are inconsistent across thread ratios: a clear win at 1/1 threads, roughly a tie at 4/4, and a clear loss at 16/16 -- the project's own README explicitly frames this as conditional, not a universal win. Single hardware sample (one laptop CPU, benchmarked Dec 2023).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh search code "than std::condition_variable" surfaced wqking/eventpp doc/policies.md ('eventpp::SpinLock has better performance than std::mutex' when threads <= core count), which links to doc/benchmark.md containing the numeric table.

name: contention_free_shared_mutex (AlexeyAB/object_threadsafe safe_ptr library)
workload: Concurrent read/write locking benchmark (bench_contfree / benchmark / CDS_test folders) comparing contention_free_shared_mutex<> to std::shared_mutex under multi-threaded mixed read/write contention on a shared object; exact operation counts and thread counts are shown only in chart images in the README, not as text/tables.
claimed_speedup: "contention_free_shared_mutex<> - 10 X times faster than std::shared_mutex" (verbatim from the repo README); illustrated with 'Performance, MOps' and 'Median Latency, usec' chart images, whose exact numeric values could not be extracted from this text-only fetch.
tradeoffs: contention_free_shared_mutex shards locking state per-thread to avoid contention, which increases memory usage relative to std::shared_mutex; safe_ptr<>/contfree_safe_ptr<> wrap objects and change access syntax (operator-> based locking) rather than being a drop-in mutex replacement; recursive-lock semantics differ from std::shared_mutex.
caveats: The '10X' figure is a first-party claim; the supporting numbers are only in embedded chart images (Performance MOps, Median Latency), not stated as text with CPU model, compiler, or flags, so this is capped at tier C. Linked CodeProject articles with fuller methodology (codeproject.com/Articles/1183423) could not be fetched to verify. Last code commit was 2020-04-13, over 6 years old -- unmaintained.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh search repos --topic lock-free --sort stars surfaced AlexeyAB/object_threadsafe (description: 'We make any object thread-safe and std::shared_mutex 10 times faster...'); confirmed via repo README.
